newsitem.title: USA: Kitty Hawk shares end lower on Boeing 727 concern.
newsitem.headline: Kitty Hawk shares end lower on Boeing 727 concern.

text.p: Kitty Hawk Inc shares fell on Friday after reports that the U.S. Federal Aviation Authority might ground Boeing 727 freight aircraft operated by the company.

The Dallas-based company's shares dropped as much as 4-1/2 to 8 in early trade but recovered to close 2-1/8 lower at 10-3/8 after company executives insisted there was little or no danger of the aircraft being pulled from service.
Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Tom Christopher told Reuters the FAA's concerns focus on the floor beams and bulkhead of 727s that have been converted for freight operations.
He said the safety questions, which do not affect Boeing 727 passenger planes, were detailed by the FAA in a November 6 internal document.

Christopher said the selling of Kitty Hawk stock was sparked by press reports that the FAA might force freight carriers to ground many of their 727s, but he said such a measure was extremely unlikely.
"It has just not been discussed to ground the airplanes. This is not a safety-of-flight item," Christopher said.

A spokesman for the FAA declined comment. "I don't think that issue is right for us to talk about right now," Assistant Administrator for Public Affairs Eliot Brenner said. He also declined to say whether FAA was studying 727s that have been converted to cargo aircraft.

Christopher said he expected the problems to be fixed quickly and cheaply. "(The FAA's) target is to come out with some sort of service bulletin during the first quarter (of 1997) for a fix on the bulkhead and the floor, and we are looking at a two- or three-day fix," Christopher said.

Christopher said strengthening the bulkhead -- the wall separating the cargo from the cockpit -- so it can withstand at least 540,000 pounds of pressure would only cost between $2,000 and $3,000 per plane.
"We anticipate we will have six months to a year to make the minor modification to the airplane," he said.
Twelve of Kitty Hawk's 26 aircraft are Boeing 727s.
